topic.name: UTI & Pyelonephritis
objectives: Differentiate cystitis vs. pyelonephritis vs. asymptomatic bacteriuria
Choose appropriate antibiotics based on local resistance patterns
Manage recurrent UTIs with prophylactic strategies
Know when to image for complicated UTIs and when to refer

content_chunks.title: Why This Matters
content_chunks.content: Sarah, 24, comes in with 3 days of burning every time she pees. She's peeing every hour, and it hurts so bad she's avoiding water. 'I get these all the time — can I just get the same antibiotic as last time?' She thinks it's no big deal. But uncomplicated UTIs are the #1 reason women see a PCP — 50-60% of women have at least one in their lifetime. Mismanage it, and that 'simple' infection can climb to the kidneys (pyelonephritis), scar them, or turn into urosepsis. 100,000 hospitalizations/year for pyelo in the US alone.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Diagram: Female urinary tract showing bacteria entering through urethra, ascending to bladder (cystitis), with red arrow showing potential further ascent to kidney (pyelonephritis)

content_chunks.title: Cystitis vs. Pyelonephritis vs. ASB
content_chunks.content:
**Uncomplicated UTI** (cystitis): Infection of the bladder in a healthy, non-pregnant, premenopausal woman with normal anatomy. Easiest to treat.

**Complicated UTI**: Risk factors that make treatment harder — male, pregnancy, diabetes, immunocompromised, renal transplant, structural abnormalities (stones, obstruction, catheters, stents), recent instrumentation, multidrug-resistant organisms. These need longer treatment and careful follow-up.

**Pyelonephritis** (kidney infection): Infection has ascended to the renal pelvis/parenchyma. More systemic, more dangerous.

**Asymptomatic Bacteriuria (ASB)**: Bacteria in the urine (≥10⁵ CFU/mL) with NO urinary symptoms. **DO NOT SCREEN OR TREAT** except in pregnancy or before urologic procedures.

| Feature | Cystitis | Pyelonephritis | ASB |
|---------|----------|---------------|-----|
| **Dysuria** | ✅ Severe | ✅ Present | ❌ |
| **Frequency/urgency** | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | ❌ |
| **Flank pain** | ❌ | ✅ Severe, unilateral | ❌ |
| **Fever/chills** | ❌ (maybe low-grade) | ✅ High (>38.5°C) | ❌ |
| **Nausea/vomiting** | ❌ | ✅ Often | ❌ |
| **Costovertebral angle tenderness** | ❌ | ✅ YES | ❌ |
| **Urgency of treatment** | Within days | IMMEDIATE! | None |

**Key Point**: If a woman has dysuria + fever + flank pain, assume PYELONEPHRITIS until proven otherwise!
content_chunks.visual_desc: Split body diagram: LEFT (cystitis): bladder with bacteria, red urethra — symptoms limited to lower tract. RIGHT (pyelonephritis): same plus red/swollen kidney with bacteria ascending ureter

content_chunks.title: 🔥 Asymptomatic Bacteriuria — DO NOT TREAT!
content_chunks.content:
**ASB is NOT a UTI!** It's colonization, not infection. Treating it causes more harm than good:
• **No benefit** — doesn't prevent symptomatic UTI or pyelonephritis
• **Harm** — drives antibiotic resistance, antibiotic side effects (C. diff!)
• **Waste** — unnecessary cost and visits

**Exceptions where treatment IS indicated**:
✅ **Pregnancy** (screen at 12-16 weeks — treat to prevent pyelo, preterm labor)
✅ **Before urologic procedures** (especially TURP, cystoscopy with mucosal breach)

**DO NOT treat** ASB in: elderly, diabetics, catheterized patients, post-menopausal women, renal transplant beyond 1 month post-op.

**Pearl**: 15-50% of elderly women and 15-30% of men >70 have ASB. If you treat their 'positive culture' you'll just get resistance + C. diff. Treat symptoms, not numbers!

mnemonics.mnemonic: **Cystitis = C**omfortable peeing (burning but no fever). **Pyelo = P**ain in back + **P**yrexia. **ASB = A**bsent **S**ymptoms = **B**ystander (don't treat!)

quick_checks.q: Which patient has asymptomatic bacteriuria that should be treated?
a: 68yo woman with positive UA, no symptoms
24yo pregnant woman at 14 weeks with positive culture, no symptoms
72yo man with catheter and positive culture
45yo diabetic woman with positive culture, no symptoms
quick_checks.explanation: ASB only treated in pregnancy (prevents pyelo/preterm labor) and before urologic procedures. Do NOT treat elderly, catheterized, or diabetic patients for ASB.

quick_checks.q: A 30yo woman has dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pain, but NO fever or flank pain. Diagnosis?
quick_checks.explanation: Lower tract symptoms only (dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pain) without fever or CVA tenderness = uncomplicated cystitis.

content_chunks.title: Acute Uncomplicated Cystitis — First-Line Abx
content_chunks.content:
**Goal**: 3-5 days of treatment. Shorter courses preferred to reduce resistance!

**First-line options** (2024 IDSA Guidelines):

**1️⃣ Nitrofurantoin** 100 mg BID × **5 days** (NOT 3!)
• **Best for**: First-line — narrow spectrum, low resistance, minimal gut flora disruption
• **Avoid**: CrCl <30 mL/min, hepatic impairment
• **Pearl**: Concentrates in urine (not blood), so won't work for pyelonephritis

**2️⃣ TMP-SMX** (Bactrim) 1 DS tab BID × **3 days**
• **Best for**: If local resistance <20% (check your local antibiogram!)
• **Avoid**: Sulfa allergy, G6PD deficiency, elderly (hyperkalemia risk), CrCl <15
• **Pearl**: Resistance is RISING — many areas now >20%, making it second-line

**3️⃣ Fosfomycin trometamol** 3 gram single dose
• **Best for**: Multidrug-resistant organisms, alternative when other options can't be used
• **Less effective** than nitrofurantoin or TMP-SMX (lower cure rates)
• **Pearl**: Good for extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) producers!

**Second-line** (if above can't be used):
• **Beta-lactams**: cephalexin 500 mg QID × 5-7 days, or amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 BID × 5-7 days
• **Fluoroquinolones** (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin): ⚠️ **RESERVED** for complicated UTI/pyelo! Avoid for simple cystitis due to side effects (tendon rupture, neuropathy, C. diff, aortic dissection) and resistance.

**Bottom line**: Nitrofurantoin 5 days = current first-line for uncomplicated cystitis.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Decision flowchart: Female with dysuria + frequency → Nitrofurantoin (first-line) → TMP-SMX (if local resistance <20%) → Fosfomycin (if MDR organism or allergy) → Beta-lactam (last resort)

content_chunks.title: Diagnostic Testing: When to Culture?
content_chunks.content:
**DO you need a urine culture?**

**❌ NO culture needed**:
• Classic uncomplicated cystitis in healthy non-pregnant woman
• Treat empirically based on typical symptoms (dysuria + frequency + urgency + no vaginitis)
• Save time, money, and reduce unnecessary antibiotic changes

**✅ YES, send culture**:
• **Complicated UTI** (male, pregnancy, diabetes, elderly, immunocompromised, stones, catheter)
• **Pyelonephritis** (always! need sensitivities for target therapy)
• **Failed treatment** (symptoms persist after 48 h on appropriate abx)
• **Recurrent UTI** (≥3 per year or ≥2 in 6 months — culture to document each episode)
• **Suspected resistant organism** (prior MDR UTI, recent abx use, travel)
• **Preoperative** (before urologic procedures)

**Interpreting the UA**:
• **Leukocyte esterase (+)** = pyuria (most sensitive: 75-96%)
• **Nitrite (+)** = enterobacteriaceae (specific: 92-100% — indicates bacteria converting nitrate to nitrite)
• **Positive both** → 92% probability of positive culture
• **Negative both** → UTI unlikely (NPV 97%)
• **WBCs on micro**: Pyuria confirms inflammation
• **False negative nitrite**: Some gram-positives (Enterococcus, Staph saprophyticus) don't produce nitrate reductase
content_chunks.visual_desc: Algorithm: Uncomplicated cystitis symptoms → NO culture → Start empiric abx. Complicated UTI, pyelo, failure, recurrence → SEND culture → Tailor abx based on sensitivities

content_chunks.title: 🔥 Staph saprophyticus — The Young Woman UTI
content_chunks.content:
**Staphylococcus saprophyticus**: The second most common cause of UTI in young, sexually active women (10-20% of cases).
• **Key clues**: Young (16-35), recently sexually active, presents with classic cystitis
• **NOT nitrite positive** (staph doesn't make nitrate reductase)
• **Treat**: Nitrofurantoin works. TMP-SMX works. Amoxicillin does NOT (resistant).

**Pregnancy UTI — SPECIAL RULES**:
• **Treat ALL positive cultures** (ASB + symptomatic) — risk of pyelo, preterm labor, low birth weight
• **Safe abx**: Nitrofurantoin (NOT in 3rd trimester — hemolytic anemia), penicillins, cephalosporins, fosfomycin
• **AVOID**: TMP (folate antagonist — risk in 1st trimester), fluoroquinolones (cartilage damage), tetracyclines
• **Duration**: 5-7 days for cystitis (longer in pregnancy)
• **Follow-up**: Test of cure — repeat culture 1-2 weeks after treatment!

**Men with UTI**:
• ALL UTIs in men are **complicated** (longer urethra → less likely to get UTI unless something else is wrong)
• Think **prostatitis**, obstruction (BPH), stones, STI
• **Workup**: DRE (prostate), UA + culture, consider PSA, imaging (post-void residual)
• **Treatment**: Fluoroquinolones or TMP-SMX × 7-14 days (prostate penetration matters)
content_chunks.visual_desc: Special populations callout box: Young women (Staph saprophyticus), Pregnant women (treat all, avoid certain drugs), Men (always complicated, think prostatitis)

quick_checks.q: Best first-line antibiotic for a 28yo non-pregnant woman with uncomplicated cystitis?
quick_checks.explanation: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg BID × 5 days is first-line for uncomplicated cystitis — narrow spectrum, low resistance, minimal microbiome disruption. Fluoroquinolones are RESERVED for pyelo/complicated UTI.

quick_checks.q: A 35yo woman returns 3 days after finishing TMP-SMX for UTI with persistent symptoms. Next step?
a: Send urine culture and switch abx based on sensitivity
quick_checks.explanation: Treatment failure = send CULTURE to guide therapy. Empiric switching without knowing resistance pattern risks continued failure. TMP-SMX resistance is common (>20% in many areas).

content_chunks.title: Why This Matters
content_chunks.content: Linda, 45, came in 4 days ago with dysuria and got nitrofurantoin. Today she's back with shaking chills, fever 39.5°C, and pain in her right flank so bad she can't stand up straight. She's nauseous and vomited twice. Her right costovertebral angle is exquisitely tender to percussion. This is pyelonephritis — the UTI has ascended to the kidney. If not treated aggressively, it can progress to **urosepsis**: hypotension, bacteremia, ICU. Pyelonephritis accounts for 250,000 ER visits and 100,000 hospitalizations yearly. You MUST recognize it early and hit hard.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Body diagram with red highlight: urethra → bladder → ureter → right kidney (swollen, inflamed, with abscess shown). Thermometer showing fever 39.5°C, hand pressing on right flank with grimace icon

content_chunks.title: Pyelonephritis — Confirming the Diagnosis
content_chunks.content:
**Clinical Diagnosis**: Fever >38°C (100.4°F) + flank pain/CVA tenderness + systemic symptoms (rigors, nausea/vomiting, malaise).

**Diagnostic criteria**:
• **UA**: WBC casts (pathognomonic — indicates renal parenchymal involvement!), pyuria, positive LE/nitrite
• **Cultures**: ALWAYS send urine culture + blood cultures (positive in 20-30% of pyelo cases)
• **Labs**: CBC (↑ WBC with left shift), BMP (check Cr — kidney function affects abx choice), blood cultures × 2

**Imaging — When to Order**:
✅ **CT abdomen/pelvis without contrast** (best test):
   • Kidneys: enlarged, perinephric stranding, delayed nephrogram
   • Can identify: abscesses, stones, obstruction, emphysematous pyelonephritis
   
✅ **Renal ultrasound**:
   • Good alternative if CT not available (pregnancy, contrast allergy)
   • Can detect hydronephrosis, stones, abscesses >2 cm

**When to image (ALL of these are indications)**:
• **No clinical improvement after 48-72 hours of appropriate antibiotics**
• **Recurrent pyelonephritis** (>2 episodes in 12 months)
• **Complicated UTI** (stones, obstruction, diabetes, immunocompromised, transplant)
• **Emphysematous pyelonephritis suspected** (gas-forming infection — diabetics!)
• **All men with pyelonephritis** (rule out obstruction, stones, abscess)
• **Severe illness** or atypical presentation
content_chunks.mnemonic: **CVAT + fever = PYELO**: **C**ostovertebral angle **T**enderness + **F**ever = **P**yelonephritis. Order UA + culture + blood cultures + consider imaging
content_chunks.visual_desc: CT scan image overlay: enlarged right kidney with perinephric stranding (inflammation), mild hydronephrosis, with left normal kidney for comparison

content_chunks.title: Treatment: Outpatient vs. Inpatient
content_chunks.content:
**OUTPATIENT** (mild-moderate, reliable patient):
**Criteria**:
• Hemodynamically stable (normal BP, HR)
• No nausea/vomiting (can tolerate PO)
• No signs of sepsis
• No pregnancy
• No complicated factors (stones, obstruction, immunocompromise)
• Reliable + can follow up in 24-48 hours

**Oral Regimens** (treat ≥14 days total):
• **Ciprofloxacin** 500 mg BID × 7 days (if resistance <10%)
• **Levofloxacin** 750 mg daily × 5 days (if resistance <10%)
• **TMP-SMX** DS BID × 14 days (if sensitivities known and susceptible)
• **Amoxicillin-clavulanate** 875/125 BID plus a fluoroquinolone if allergy concerns

**INPATIENT** (moderate-severe or complicated):
**Admit if**:
• SBP <90 or HR >120
• High fever >39.5°C
• Intractable vomiting/dehydration
• Pregnancy (admit ALL pregnant pyelo patients!)
• Immunocompromised
• Renal transplant
• Age >65 with comorbidities
• Suspected obstruction (stone, stricture)
• Failed oral therapy
• Signs of sepsis/SIRS (temp >38 or <36, HR >90, RR >20, WBC >12K or <4K)

**IV Regimens** (switch to PO when afebrile × 24-48 hours):
• **Ceftriaxone** 1 gram IV daily (most common — covers most gram-negatives)
• **Cefepime** 1 gram IV q12h (if pseudomonas risk)
• **Piperacillin-tazobactam** (Zosyn) 3.375 g IV q6h (broad spectrum)
• **Gentamicin/tobramycin** (aminoglycosides) — nephrotoxic, used with caution
• **Fluoroquinolones** IV if no contraindications

**Total duration**: 14 days for all pyelonephritis (IV + PO combined). Treat until afebrile for 24-48 hours, then complete course orally.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Decision tree: Pyelonephritis diagnosis → Assess severity (SBP <90, fever >39.5, vomiting, pregnancy, etc.) → YES to any = ADMIT (IV abx). NO to all = Outpatient (PO abx, follow up in 24-48h)

content_chunks.title: Recurrent UTI — Prophylaxis Strategies
content_chunks.content:
**Definition**: ≥3 culture-documented UTIs per year OR ≥2 in 6 months.

**Step 1 — Confirm it's real**:
✅ Document each episode with culture (don't rely on symptoms alone)
✅ Rule out complicated factors (imaging if recurrent)
✅ Exclude STI mimics (chlamydia, gonorrhea, trichomonas, mycoplasma)
✅ Check for vaginitis: bacterial vaginosis, yeast — dysuria can be from vaginitis, not UTI!

**Step 2 — Behavioral modifications**:
✅ **Hydrate!** — aim for 2-3 L/day
✅ **Void after intercourse** (reduces risk 30-50%)
✅ **Wipe front to back** (always!)
✅ **Avoid spermicides** (alter vaginal flora → ↑ UTI risk)
✅ **Consider D-mannose** 2 g daily (some data showing reduction in recurrent UTI)
✅ **Cranberry** (Vaccinium macrocarpon) — proanthocyanidins prevent bacterial adherence. Useful for PREVENTION (not treatment). 500 mg daily or 8 oz unsweetened juice. Modest benefit.

**Step 3 — Prophylactic antibiotics** (if behavioral measures fail):

**Continuous prophylaxis** (for ≥3 UTIs/year — take for 6-12 months):
• **Nitrofurantoin** 50-100 mg nightly
• **TMP-SMX** ½ SS tab nightly
• **Cephalexin** 125-250 mg nightly
• **Norfloxacin** 200 mg nightly (reserved)

**Post-coital prophylaxis** (if UTIs clearly linked to intercourse):
• Take ONE dose within 2 hours after sex
• Same abx options as above
• Less total antibiotic exposure than continuous!

**Self-start therapy** (reliable patient with clear symptoms):
• Prescribe a 3-day course of abx to keep at home
• Patient starts at first symptoms, reports to clinic within 72 hours
• Good for patients who recognize UTI symptoms clearly

**Step 4 — Non-antibiotic options**:
• **Vaginal estrogen** (post-menopausal women!) — restores vaginal lactobacilli, reduces pH, ↓ UTI risk dramatically. FIRST-LINE for post-menopausal recurrent UTI!
• **D-Mannose** 2 g daily — some evidence
• **Methenamine hippurate** — converts to formaldehyde in acidic urine (bacteriostatic, modest benefit)
content_chunks.visual_desc: Pyramid: Base (behavioral: hydrate, void post-coital, front-to-back) → Middle (prophylactic abx: continuous or post-coital) → Top (advanced: vaginal estrogen for post-menopausal, D-mannose, self-start therapy)

mnemonics.mnemonic: **SICK-P** — **S**epsis signs (hypotension, tachycardia), **I**ntractable vomiting, **C**omplicated (stones, obstruction), **K**idney transplant / immunocompromised, **P**regnancy
**BE-VEST**: **B**ehavior changes → **E**strogen (vaginal) → **V**oid post-coital → **E**very night abx → **S**elf-start therapy → **T**ake imaging

quick_checks.q: Which patient with pyelonephritis can be treated as an OUTPATIENT?
a: 28yo healthy woman, fever 38.2°C, mild flank pain, no vomiting
45yo man with flank pain and obstruction on imaging
quick_checks.explanation: Outpatient candidates must be: hemodynamically stable, non-pregnant, no vomiting, no complicated factors, reliable for follow-up. Pregnancy, high fever, diabetes + age >65, and obstruction all require admission.

quick_checks.q: Best first-line prophylaxis for a 68yo post-menopausal woman with 4 UTIs in the past year?
quick_checks.explanation: Vaginal estrogen is FIRST-LINE in post-menopausal women — restores vaginal lactobacilli, reduces pH, and dramatically reduces UTI risk. Try non-antibiotic options first before committing to daily antibiotic prophylaxis!
